meta.project: Rental Increase Review — San Francisco, Outer Sunset, ZIP 94122
meta.built_note: All sources retrieved and read directly on 2026-11-06 (UTC).

sections.title: San Francisco law
sections.subtitle: Administrative Code Chapter 37 (Rent Ordinance), Rent Board Rules and Regulations, and Rent Board published rates
sections.intro: San Francisco's local cap is the binding constraint on both units. Where the local cap is lower than the state cap, the local cap governs the tenancy.

rows.claim: Rent control applies to most residential units built on or before June 13, 1979.
rows.detail: Rent Board: "Many residential units built on or before June 13, 1979 have both rent control and eviction protection." Units built after that date, most single-family homes and condos, substantially rehabilitated units and certain subsidized units do not have rent control.
rows.note: A 1940 building is before the cutoff. The build year alone does not by itself prove coverage — a single-family-dwelling or Costa-Hawkins partial exemption would have to be ruled out; a 2-unit building that is not a condominium or a house is not one of those exemptions.

rows.claim: The allowable annual rent increase for 3/1/2026 – 2/28/2027 is 1.6% of base rent.
rows.detail: Rent Board document 571: "Effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, the allowable annual increase amount is 1.6%." Multiply base rent by .016.
rows.note: Independently confirmed by the Rent Board news item of 14 Jan 2026 and by the Current Rates page.

rows.claim: The prior period allowance was 1.4% (3/1/2025 – 2/28/2026).
rows.note: Relevant to Unit 1, whose increase opportunity fell on 1 Feb 2026 while 1.4% was the rate in effect.

rows.claim: The annual allowance is 60% of the published CPI increase, and can never exceed 7%.
rows.detail: Rent Ordinance sec. 37.3(a)(1): a licensed landlord "shall have a license to impose annually a rent increase which does not exceed a tenant's base rent by more than 60% of said published increase. In no event, however, shall the allowable annual increase be greater than 7%."
rows.note: Rule 1.12 (amended 1/13/2026) adds the rounding method and the geometric-mean workaround for the unpublished October 2025 CPI.

rows.claim: Rent may be increased only once every 12 months, measured from the anniversary date.
rows.detail: Rent Board: "a landlord can only increase a tenant's rent by a certain percentage once every 12 months." The first annual increase may be imposed 12 months after the lease began.
rows.note: If the increase is imposed later than 12 months, the date it is imposed becomes the new anniversary date.

rows.claim: The increase is computed on base rent only, and may not be rounded up.
rows.detail: "Landlords must calculate the rent increase on the tenant's base rent only. This includes any housing services like parking or storage. It does not include any temporary passthroughs or fluctuating charges. Rent increases cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar."
rows.value: Base rent only; no rounding up
rows.note: Rule 4.12 repeats the no-rounding rule for banked amounts.

rows.claim: A landlord must hold a Rent Board rent increase license before an annual or banked increase takes effect.
rows.detail: Ordinance sec. 37.15(e): a landlord who has substantially complied with Housing Inventory reporting "shall receive a license to impose rent increases"; if not, the licence is suspended and "a tenant shall not be obligated to pay the increased rent for months during the period of suspension."
rows.note: Operative July 1, 2022, or March 1, 2023 for condominiums and buildings with 1-9 residential units — which includes a 2-unit building. The licence need not be attached to the notice, but the notice is unenforceable without it on the effective date.

rows.claim: 30 days' written notice is required; 90 days if the increase is more than 10%; add 5 days if the notice is mailed.
rows.detail: Rent Board: "30-day written notice" and "90-day written notice if the increase (either by itself or combined with another increase in the same year) is more than 10%." "If the notice is mailed, the landlord must give the tenant 5 more days."
rows.note: Rule 4.10 makes a non-conforming notice void, subject to a narrow good-faith 0.5% adjustment.

rows.claim: The notice must state the dollar amount, the percentage, the effective date, and which part is banked.
rows.detail: Rent Board lists the required contents and adds: "The landlord should use the percentage that will be in effect on the date of the increase, not the percentage in effect on the date they serve the notice."
rows.note: Ordinance sec. 37.3(b)(5): any increase that does not conform "shall be null and void."

rows.claim: An increase that does not comply is null and void in its entirety.
rows.detail: Rule 4.10(b): "Any rent increase which does not conform with the provisions of this Section shall render the entire rent increase null and void", except where the overage is no more than 0.5% of prior base rent and given in good faith.
rows.note: Ordinance sec. 37.3(b)(5) says the same in the Ordinance text.

rows.claim: Unused annual increases may be accumulated and imposed later, are not compounded, and are not rounded up.
rows.detail: Ordinance sec. 37.3(a)(2) and Rule 4.12: a landlord who refrains from imposing an increase may accumulate it; only increases available on or after April 1, 1982 may be banked; "Banked increases shall not be compounded and shall not be rounded up."
rows.note: Rent Board's summary adds: no cap on the amount banked, banked increases do not expire during a tenancy, a new owner may use a prior owner's banked amounts, and banked amounts do not carry to a new tenant.

rows.claim: Banked percentages are added together, then applied once to current base rent.
rows.detail: Rent Board worked example: tenant moved in 8/1/2022 at $1,300; landlord first raises rent on 8/1/2025. Banked 3.6% + 1.7% = 5.3%, plus 1.4% annual = 6.7%; $1,300 x .067 = $87.10.
rows.note: Confirms the method used for Unit 2 in this review.

rows.claim: Two official Rent Board pages state different waiting periods before a skipped increase may be banked.
rows.detail: Rule 4.12 (the adopted regulation, doc 625, amended through 1/13/2026): "A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable." The Rent Board's plain-language page says: "A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase."
rows.note: FLAGGED. The regulation and the summary page disagree. Both sources are official. This does not change the Unit 2 result, because every year used for Unit 2 is more than 24 months old. It would change results for a single recently-skipped year. Resolve by calling a Rent Board counselor (415-252-4600) before relying on banking for a recent year.

rows.claim: Where no increase has been imposed for two or more years, the allowable percentages for the intervening years may be added.
rows.detail: Rent Board: "landlords may increase rent by adding up the allowable increases during that time period"; work 8.2% = 2.2 + 1.6 + 2.6 + 1.8. "Increases cannot be compounded." No petition is required.
rows.note: Directly supports the Unit 2 calculation.

rows.claim: Adding a roommate or occupant is not a lawful basis for a rent increase.
rows.detail: Rent Board: "A landlord cannot charge additional rent simply because a new (or additional) roommate has moved into a unit with the existing tenant. This is an unlawful rent increase, even if the lease or rental agreement provides for the additional charge." Ordinance sec. 37.3(a)(11) says the same.
rows.note: Directly relevant: Unit 1 gained occupant P4 on 2026-04-01 while rent stayed at $3,995.

rows.claim: Any increase above the allowable annual and banked amount requires a Rent Board petition.
rows.detail: Six increase types require a petition before the notice is served: capital improvement passthrough; operating and maintenance expense; special circumstances / comparable rents; Prop I past rent history; utility passthrough; Rule 1.21 increase. Tenants need not pay until the Board approves, and approval is retroactive to a valid notice date.
rows.note: Ordinance sec. 37.3(a)(8): a landlord seeking more "shall petition for a rental arbitration hearing."

rows.claim: A tenant may petition at any time, at no charge, to have the lawful rent determined.
rows.detail: Form 516C with Form C. "There is no time limit for filing a petition" and "There is no charge for filing the petition." A 518 Tenant Summary Petition exists for a notice that is "clearly unlawful on its face" and usually triggers a corrected notice without a hearing.
rows.note: This is the mechanism by which any increase will be tested if a tenant disputes it.

rows.claim: Tenants cannot get hardship deferral of an annual or banked increase.
rows.detail: Hardship relief is limited to capital improvement passthroughs, water revenue bond passthroughs, general obligation bond passthroughs, utility passthroughs and O&M increases. "For all other types of rent increases or passthroughs, including annual and banked rent increases ... financial hardship relief is not available."
rows.note: So a hardship argument does not defeat a compliant annual increase, but it does defeat the passthrough types.

rows.claim: A bad-faith rent increase intended to make a tenant vacate is tenant harassment.
rows.detail: Ordinance sec. 37.10B(a)(5) covers influencing a tenant to vacate "through fraud, intimidation or coercion", including a rent increase intended to coerce; the section lists a rent increase "substantially in excess of market rates for comparable units" as evidence. Remedies include treble damages, statutory damages of $1,000, and attorney's fees.
rows.note: This is the statutory hook a tenant-side lawyer would use against an aggressive increase. It is a bad-faith standard, not a cap.

rows.claim: A tenant may sue over excess rent, and the prevailing party recovers attorney's fees.
rows.detail: Ordinance sec. 37.11A(a): where a landlord charges rent above the Chapter 37 limits, the tenant may seek injunctive relief and damages, and "in cases where the landlord has charged an excessive rent in violation of Section 37.9B(a)", damages of not less than three times the excess. Sec. 37.11A(c): "The prevailing party ... shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorneys' fees and costs."
rows.note: Read carefully: the treble-damages language is tied to sec. 37.9B(a), not to every overcharge. Ordinary overpayment recovery is limited to a three-year lookback.

rows.claim: San Francisco forbids landlords from using algorithmic devices to set rents.
rows.detail: Ordinance sec. 37.10C (added by Ord. 224-24, effective 10/14/2024; amended 10/6/2025) makes it unlawful to sell or use revenue-management software that calculates non-public competitor data to recommend rents or occupancy. Each month and each unit is a separate violation; penalties up to $1,000 per violation plus fees.
rows.note: Rules out the institutional revenue-management approach as a lawful method in San Francisco.

rows.claim: The 2026-27 Rent Board fee is $59.00 per dwelling unit, and up to 50% may be recovered from a qualifying tenant.
rows.detail: "For the 2026-2027 tax year, the fee is $59.00 per dwelling unit ... If you pay the Rent Board fee in full, you may be able to collect 50% of the fee from your tenants, which is $29.50 per dwelling unit." Due March 1; 5% penalty per month up to 15%.
rows.note: This is a fee recovery, not a rent increase, and belongs on a separate billing statement.

rows.claim: The fee may only be billed to a tenant who was in occupancy on or before November 1 of the prior year, and not as a rent increase.
rows.detail: Recover by deducting from security deposit interest due, or by separate bill (only if no or insufficient deposit). The bill must state the amount, that its purpose is to fund the Rent Board, and that it is due within 30 days. Non-payment of the fee is not just cause for eviction.
rows.note: For Unit 1, P4 arrived 2026-04-01 and would fail the November 1 test for the fee due 3/1/2027.

rows.claim: An unlimited increase on remaining occupants is available only when the last original occupant has vacated.
rows.detail: Rule 6.14 allows an unlimited increase "when the last original occupant vacates the unit", provided a written 6.14 notice was timely served on each subsequent occupant (generally within 60 days). A co-tenant — as opposed to a subtenant — is not subject to a Costa-Hawkins market-rate increase regardless of when the co-tenant moved in.
rows.value: Only after last original tenant leaves
rows.note: Unit 1 still has an original tenant (P1) in occupancy, so this route is not available. It also means the April 2026 addition of P4 did not reset or unlock anything.

rows.claim: Landlords must meet and confer in good faith with a certified Tenant Association, including about rent increases; a 2-unit building cannot certify one.
rows.detail: Admin Code ch. 49A: a Tenant Association requires "a building with five or more rental units" and a petition signed by tenants of at least 50% of occupied units. Landlords "shall confer ... in good faith regarding ... rent increases".
rows.note: The formal duty does not attach to a 2-unit building, but the good-faith-communication norm in the chapter is still the standard a reviewer will apply informally.

rows.claim: Rent increases in ZIP 94122 are actually contested: 42 tenant petitions and 15 capital improvement petitions were filed from that ZIP in FY 2024-25.
rows.detail: Rent Board Annual Statistical Report FY 2024-2025: tenant petitions by ZIP — 94122 Sunset 42; capital improvement petitions by ZIP — 94122 Sunset 15. Citywide total tenant petitions 880; total landlord petitions 339.
rows.note: Useful context: this is not a theoretical risk. The Sunset is an active filing area.

sections.title: California law
sections.subtitle: Civil Code notice and rent-cap statutes, and the Attorney General's published cap tables
sections.intro: State law sets a procedural floor (notice) and a statewide cap. Where a local ordinance is stricter, the local cap displaces the state cap.

rows.claim: Civil Code 827 requires 30 days' notice for an increase of 10% or less, and 90 days for an increase greater than 10%, measured against the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months.
rows.detail: Sec. 827(b)(2)-(3): 30 days if the increase is 10 percent or less "either in and of itself or when combined with any other rent increases for the 12 months before the effective date"; 90 days if greater than 10 percent.
rows.note: Same 90-day threshold as the Rent Board's page, so there is no local/state conflict here.

rows.claim: Notice must be delivered personally, or by mail following Code of Civil Procedure 1013.
rows.detail: Sec. 827(b)(1): "(A) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (B) By serving a copy by mail under the procedures prescribed in Section 1013 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
rows.note: Sec. 827(c): if another statute or a recorded regulatory agreement requires a longer notice period, the longer period applies.

rows.claim: The Tenant Protection Act caps increases at 5% plus the change in cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12 months.
rows.detail: Sec. 1947.12(a)(1), measured against the lowest gross rent charged in the prior 12 months; no more than two increments in 12 months (a)(2).
rows.note: Not the operative cap here, because sec. 1947.12(d)(3) exempts housing subject to a local ordinance that restricts increases to less than the state amount.

rows.claim: The state cap does not apply where a local ordinance restricts annual increases to less than the state cap.
rows.detail: Sec. 1947.12(d)(3): "Housing subject to rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police power ... that restricts annual increases in the rental rate to an amount less than that provided in subdivision (a)."
rows.note: Practical result: for these units the ceiling is 1.6% (plus properly banked amounts), not 8.8%.

rows.claim: The Attorney General publishes 8.8% for the San Francisco area for increases starting 8/1/2026 – 7/31/2027.
rows.detail: AG table, San Francisco Area (Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Francisco, San Mateo): 6.3% for 8/1/25-7/31/26; 8.8% for 8/1/26-7/31/27. The AG page then states that where a local cap is lower, "the local rule will apply."
rows.note: This is the number a landlord might see quoted in the press. It is the wrong number for a rent-controlled San Francisco unit.

rows.claim: The state rent cap exempts a two-unit structure where the owner occupied one unit at the start of the tenancy and still does.
rows.detail: Sec. 1947.12(d)(6): "A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner's principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy..."
rows.note: Both units are rented, so this exemption does not apply. Also note it is a state-cap exemption only; it does not remove the local ordinance.

rows.claim: Costa-Hawkins allows an owner to set initial and subsequent rates for separately alienable units, subject to exceptions.
rows.detail: Sec. 1954.52(a)(3) applies to a dwelling "alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit", but not where the preceding tenancy was terminated on notice under 1946.1 or by a change in terms under 827.
rows.note: FLAGGED as fact-dependent. Two units in one 1940 structure are normally not separately alienable unless the building has been condominium-converted. The title structure was not provided, so no exemption is assumed.

rows.claim: When a unit is truly vacant and no prior tenant remains, the owner may set the initial rent, and the cap then applies to later increases.
rows.detail: Sec. 1954.53(a); sec. 1947.12(b) is to the same effect for the state cap.
rows.note: Not available for either unit — both are occupied. This is the route that resets the base rent, and it requires a genuinely empty unit.

rows.claim: A rent increase within 180 days of a tenant's habitability complaint or tenant-organising activity is prohibited, and attorney's fees are available.
rows.detail: Sec. 1942.5(a) bars increasing rent within 180 days of a good-faith repair notice or complaint to an agency; (d) bars increases for retaliating against organising; (h) sets damages including punitive damages of $100-$2,000 per act; (i) provides attorney's fees to the prevailing party.
rows.note: Practical rule: check the repair-complaint log before setting an effective date.

rows.claim: After 12 months of tenancy an owner may not terminate without just cause stated in the notice.
rows.detail: Sec. 1946.2(a); if additional adult tenants are added before an existing tenant reaches 24 months, the 12-month clock requires all tenants to reach 12 months or one tenant to reach 24 months.
rows.note: Relevant to Unit 1, where P4 joined in April 2026: the just-cause clock is affected by the addition, which is a reason not to treat the tenancy as new.

rows.claim: A residential lease over one month negotiated primarily in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean requires a translated copy before signing.
rows.detail: Sec. 1632(b)(3) covers "a lease, sublease, rental contract or agreement ... for a period of longer than one month, covering a dwelling."
rows.note: Applies to a new or renewed lease, not to a bare rent-increase notice — but a new lease handed over with a renewal should carry a translation if negotiated in a covered language.

rows.claim: The Fair Employment and Housing Act bars discrimination in housing on 16 listed characteristics, including source of income and familial status.
rows.detail: Gov. Code 12955(a): race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, genetic information.
rows.note: Adds state characteristics — notably source of income and marital status — that are not in the federal list.

rows.claim: The October 2025 San Francisco CPI was never published, because of the 2025 lapse in federal appropriations.
rows.detail: BLS release: the October 2025 data values in the year-over-year table are "not available due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations". BLS does publish April 2026 at 3.8% and August 2026 at 3.4% for the San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward area.
rows.note: Explains why Rule 1.12 was amended: the Rent Board now approximates the missing October 2025 figure by geometric mean of August and December 2025.

sections.title: Federal law
sections.subtitle: Fair Housing Act, HUD regulation, antitrust enforcement, and the absence of a federal rent cap
sections.intro: There is no federal rent-control statute governing a private San Francisco tenancy. The federal constraints that do apply are the Fair Housing Act (including disparate-impact liability) and the antitrust laws as applied to rent-setting software.

rows.claim: No federal statute or regulation caps the rent a private landlord may charge on an unassisted San Francisco unit.
rows.detail: No such provision was located in the sources reviewed. The federal rent-related instruments identified in this review are the Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. 3601 et seq.), the HUD fair-market-rent mechanism, and the antitrust laws.
rows.note: FLAGGED. An absence cannot be proven by citation, so this is recorded as unverified rather than asserted. It is consistent with the Rent Board and Attorney General pages, which describe only local and state caps as binding.

rows.claim: It is unlawful to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status or national origin.
rows.detail: 42 U.S.C. 3604(b): "To discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling ... because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin."
rows.note: This is the provision that a differential rent between two otherwise comparable units is tested against — not a rule that rents must be identical.

rows.claim: The FHA applies to these units: the small-owner exemptions do not fit a non-owner-occupied two-unit building.
rows.detail: 42 U.S.C. 3603(b)(1) exempts a single-family house rented by a private owner of no more than three such houses; (b)(2) exempts rooms or units in a dwelling of no more than four families "if the owner actually maintains and occupies one of such living quarters as his residence".
rows.note: Both exemptions require either a single-family house or owner occupancy. Neither is present. Also, 3603(b) does not exempt 3604(c) — discriminatory statements — in any event.

rows.claim: Liability can attach for a discriminatory effect even without discriminatory intent, subject to a legally sufficient justification.
rows.detail: 24 C.F.R. 100.500: a practice has a discriminatory effect where it "actually or predictably results in a disparate impact on a group of persons or creates, increases, reinforces, or perpetuates segregated housing patterns". A justification must be necessary to a substantial, legitimate, non-discriminatory interest, supported by evidence, and not achievable by a less discriminatory alternative.
rows.note: This is why an inconsistent pattern matters even if the motive is clean: the theory does not require proof of intent.

rows.claim: The Department of Justice obtained a consent judgment requiring RealPage to stop using competitors' non-public data to set rents.
rows.detail: DOJ release 25-1111 (24 Nov 2025): RealPage must cease using competitors' non-public competitively sensitive information in runtime operation; limit model training to data aged at least 12 months; not model geography narrower than state level; remove features limiting price decreases or aligning pricing; accept a court-appointed monitor; and cooperate against landlord defendants.
rows.note: Combined with SF Ordinance 37.10C, revenue-management software is not a usable method in San Francisco and is an antitrust exposure federally.

rows.claim: HUD fair market rents are 40th-percentile gross rent estimates used to set voucher payment standards. They are not a rent cap and are not a market-rent benchmark for a private increase.
rows.detail: HUD USER: FMRs "are estimates of 40th percentile gross rents for standard quality units within a metropolitan area or nonmetropolitan county" under 24 CFR 888.113, used for Housing Choice Voucher payment standards, project-based Section 8 renewals, HOME rent ceilings, and public housing flat rents.
rows.note: The numeric FY2026 two-bedroom figure for the San Francisco metro did not render on the HUD documentation page, so no dollar value is published on this site. FLAGGED as unverified.

rows.claim: The federal protected classes are race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status and national origin.
rows.detail: 42 U.S.C. 3602 definitions of handicap (physical or mental impairment substantially limiting a major life activity, a record of one, or being regarded as having one) and familial status (a person under 18 domiciled with a parent or custodian).
rows.note: California adds source of income, marital status, ancestry, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status and genetic information.

sections.title: How increases are actually handled
sections.subtitle: Institutional owners, individual San Francisco owners, and what a defensible notice looks like
sections.intro: Read this page as evidence, not advice: what large operators say in their own SEC filings, what the Rent Board forms and rules actually require, and which stated reasons are supportable.

rows.claim: A large single-family rental REIT states that it sets rents using a pricing tool built on publicly available data plus property-specific factors.
rows.detail: Invitation Homes 2025 Form 10-K: associates set rates "based on a tailored pricing tool that analyzes publicly available data to reflect local market conditions, including a competitive analysis of market rents for institutional single-family rental properties, as well as the size, fit and finish, and location of the home, the number of applications received, and the number of days a home has been available on the market."
rows.note: Note the stated data posture — publicly available data. After DOJ v. RealPage and SF Ord. 37.10C, the non-public-data model is the liability.

rows.claim: Institutional renewal increases are driven by portfolio revenue targets, not by the local rent-control formula.
rows.detail: AvalonBay 2025 annual report: 2025 same-store residential revenue growth 2.5%, same-store residential NOI growth 1.9%; the 2026 outlook assumes same-store residential revenue growth of 1.4% and notes record resident retention.
rows.note: These are portfolio-level growth figures across many markets, not the size of any individual renewal increase. They are not a lawful benchmark for a rent-controlled San Francisco unit.

rows.claim: The largest operators hold tens of thousands of units and standardise leases, screening and pricing centrally.
rows.detail: Invitation Homes 10-K: 86,192 single-family properties as of 31 Dec 2025, and the platform allows it to "standardize resident leases, employ a consistent approach to resident screening and leasing operations, and utilize a tailored pricing tool".
rows.note: Scale is what makes centralised pricing possible. A two-unit owner has no portfolio to optimise and no equivalent data set.

rows.claim: Institutional filers treat rent-regulation limits as a disclosed risk factor.
rows.detail: Invitation Homes 10-K risk factor: "Eviction, tenant rights, rent control, and rent stabilization laws, and other similar laws and/or regulations that limit our ability to collect rent, enforce remedies for failure to pay rent, or increase rental rates may negatively impact our rental income and profitability."
rows.note: Confirms the regulated-owner framing: the cap is the operating constraint, not a negotiation position.

rows.claim: An individual San Francisco owner's lawful method is to apply the published percentage, hold a licence, serve the statutory notice, and document the base rent.
rows.detail: The Rent Board sets out a complete procedure: confirm coverage; report into the Housing Inventory to obtain the rent increase licence; compute 1.6% (or 1.6% plus banked percentages) on base rent with no rounding up; serve 30 days' notice (90 if over 10%) stating dollar amount, percentage and effective date; and identify which portion is annual and which is banked.
rows.note: There is no filing, and no fee, for an annual or banked increase within the allowance.

rows.claim: For an annual or banked increase within the allowance, no justification or reason beyond the ordinance formula is required.
rows.detail: The Rent Board describes the annual increase as imposable "without filing a petition" (doc 571) and requires only the percentage and dollar figures, not a reason. Reasons and cost documentation become mandatory only for petition-based increases, which must be filed "on the forms provided by the Rent Board" and "must include supporting documentation".
rows.note: Practical point: adding a cost narrative to an annual increase is optional; adding one that misstates the basis is a risk you did not need to take.

rows.claim: Several commonly offered justifications are unlawful in San Francisco.
rows.detail: Not permitted: an increase because a roommate or family member moved in (Ord. 37.3(a)(11)); an increase in bad faith to induce the tenant to leave (Ord. 37.10B(a)(5)); an increase within 180 days of a habitability complaint (Civ. Code 1942.5); an increase calculated with revenue-management software (Ord. 37.10C); an increase that has not been computed on base rent only, or that has been rounded up.
rows.note: Each of these is a separate, independently sourced defect.

rows.claim: The defensible basis for these units is the published allowance plus documented banked percentages, tied to the tenancy's own anniversary date.
rows.detail: Because the allowance is fixed by the Board and applied to each tenancy's own base rent and anniversary date, the reason for the increase is the ordinance, and the explanation is arithmetic. That explanation is auditable from public sources.
rows.note: Where the two units receive different dollar increases, the lawful explanation is the difference in anniversary dates and banked years — not the identity of the tenants.

rows.claim: Keep proof of service and a copy of the notice; the tenant can request a full rent history review at no cost and with no deadline.
rows.detail: Service must be personal or by mail under CCP 1013 (Civ. Code 827(b)(1)). The Rent Board accepts a 516C petition at any time, free, and Form C asks for the complete rent history, receipts and cancelled cheques.
rows.note: A clean file — lease, every notice, every increase, the licence record — is the whole of the defence.

rows.claim: The Rent Board offers free counseling and will answer these questions directly, and it publishes a referral list rather than endorsing individual lawyers.
rows.detail: "The Rent Board cannot refer you to individual attorneys, but staff will be glad to direct you to appropriate resources." Counseling is by phone on 415-252-4600, weekday mornings and afternoons.
rows.note: A counseling call logged before serving notice is the cheapest available verification step.

sections.title: Review test — one unit or both
sections.subtitle: The checklist a tenant-side lawyer would run, and the analysis of raising one unit versus both
sections.intro: This page is a stress test, not a legal opinion. Each checklist item is tied to the text that creates the risk. The one-unit-versus-both question is answered with the reasoning shown, and the limits of that reasoning are flagged.

rows.claim: Is the unit covered by the Rent Ordinance?
rows.detail: Built 1940; two units; not a single-family dwelling; no substantial rehabilitation claimed. Coverage follows from the June 13, 1979 cutoff.
rows.note: Confirm the certificate of occupancy on the Planning Property Information Map before serving notice.

rows.claim: Does the landlord hold a current rent increase licence for each unit?
rows.detail: Report into the Housing Inventory; a licence is generated for tenant-occupied units. Without it the increase is unenforceable for the suspension period and the tenant need not pay.
rows.note: UNVERIFIED in this review: no licence status was provided. This is the first thing to check in the Portal.

rows.claim: Is the percentage no more than the allowance in effect on the effective date?
rows.detail: 1.6% for effective dates from 3/1/2026; 1.4% for effective dates 3/1/2025-2/28/2026. Use the rate in effect on the effective date, not the notice date.

rows.claim: Were banked percentages computed without compounding, and identified as banked in the notice?
rows.detail: Rule 4.12(b) requires the notice to state which portion is banked and the dates the banked amount is based on. Failure to include that information does not void the increase, but it is the cheapest defect to avoid.

rows.claim: Is the arithmetic on base rent only, with no rounding up?
rows.detail: Neither notice may round the increase or the resulting base rent up to a whole dollar.
rows.note: For Unit 2, both rent levels and the increase should be expressed to the cent.

rows.claim: Is the notice period at least 30 days, and at least 90 days where the increase exceeds 10%?
rows.detail: Unit 2's calculated increase is 13.1%, which crosses the 10% threshold and requires 90 days. Unit 1's alternatives are below 10% and require 30 days.
rows.note: Add 5 days if served by mail, per the Rent Board's statement.

rows.claim: Is the effective date at least 12 months after the last increase or the tenancy start?
rows.detail: Unit 1: 2/1/2025 lease start, so the earliest allowable date was 2/1/2026. Unit 2: 6/1/2019 start, so the earliest allowable date was 6/1/2020.
rows.note: If an increase is imposed late, that late date becomes the new anniversary date.

rows.claim: Is there any retaliation flag in the last 180 days?
rows.detail: A rent increase within 180 days of a repair request, habitability complaint, agency complaint, or organising activity is prohibited by Civ. Code 1942.5, with a fee-shifting exposure.
rows.note: UNVERIFIED in this review: no repair or complaint history was provided.

rows.claim: Is the increase free of any discriminatory selection effect?
rows.detail: The FHA reaches disparate impact without intent. The test is whether the pattern of who receives an increase, and how much, tracks a protected characteristic rather than a lawful variable such as anniversary date or banked years.

rows.claim: Is the amount defensible against a bad-faith / harassment characterisation?
rows.detail: Ord. 37.10B(a)(5) treats a rent increase used to influence a tenant to vacate as harassment, and lists a rent increase substantially above comparable-unit market rates as evidence. An increase at or under the published allowance does not present that profile.

rows.claim: Neither the Rent Ordinance nor the FHA requires that two units receive the same increase.
rows.detail: No provision reviewed requires uniform treatment across units. The FHA prohibits discrimination because of a protected characteristic; it does not impose a most-favoured-tenant rule. The Rent Board computes the allowance per tenancy, from that tenancy's own base rent and anniversary date.
rows.note: FLAGGED as an inference from the structure of the ordinance rather than a quoted prohibition. It is a strong inference — the computation is tenancy-specific by design — but it is not a cited holding.

rows.claim: Because the two tenancies have different anniversary dates and different banked histories, different increases are the arithmetically correct outcome.
rows.detail: Unit 1's first opportunity fell on 2/1/2026 at 1.4%. Unit 2 has never been increased since 6/1/2019 and has accumulated 13.1% in non-compounded allowances. Applying the same percentage to both would itself be the arithmetic error.
rows.note: This is the documentable, non-discriminatory reason for any difference: a stated rule applied uniformly.

rows.claim: The discrimination risk is highest when the treated group is small and the distinction is unexplained.
rows.detail: With two units, a differential can look like selection. The mitigation is a written record created before the notices: the same method applied to both, the same notice template, the same effective-date logic, and a short written basis for each number.
rows.note: FLAGGED as risk management judgement, not a citation. It follows from the disparate-impact standard in F04 rather than from any single rule.

rows.claim: Withholding a lawful increase from one unit is not itself unlawful, but it creates its own record problem.
rows.detail: A landlord may impose less than the allowance, and the unused portion banks (Ord. 37.3(a)(2); Rule 4.12). So declining to increase one unit does not forfeit the entitlement — it converts it into a banked amount that can be imposed later.
rows.note: This is the honest answer to "is it safer to raise only one": the exposure is not the increase you did not serve, it is the unexplained difference when you later serve it.

rows.claim: Recommended course: apply the same method to both units, and record the calculation for each.
rows.detail: Serve each unit the allowance its own anniversary date and history supports; use one notice template; attach a one-page calculation showing base rent, rate, banked years and arithmetic; keep proof of service; and log a counseling call with the Rent Board beforehand.
rows.note: FLAGGED as a recommendation. It is a procedure assembled from verified requirements, not a legal opinion. It is what makes the file reviewable.

rows.topic: What a lawyer will look for
rows.claim: A reviewer can invalidate the whole increase on a single formal defect.
rows.detail: Ordinance 37.3(b)(5) and Rule 4.10(b): a non-conforming increase is null and void in its entirety, subject only to a good-faith adjustment of up to 0.5% of prior base rent. The defect does not have to be large.
rows.note: This is why the notice content matters more than the percentage.

sections.title: Worked calculations
sections.subtitle: Unit 1 and Unit 2, computed from the facts provided and the published allowances
sections.intro: The arithmetic below uses only the published Rent Board percentages and the base rents stated in the brief. Every unknown is left as a flag rather than filled in. Nothing here has been served on any tenant; these are scenarios.

rows.claim: Anniversary date and earliest lawful increase date.
rows.detail: Lease start 1 Feb 2025 at $3,995. The first annual increase could be imposed from 1 Feb 2026. The rate in effect on 1 Feb 2026 was 1.4%.
rows.note: Whether an increase was actually imposed on 1 Feb 2026 was not provided. FLAGGED.

rows.claim: Scenario A — increase effective 1 Feb 2026 at 1.4%.
rows.note: Arithmetic on the stated base rent. Not rounded up.

rows.claim: Scenario B — increase effective on or after 1 Mar 2026 at 1.6%.
rows.note: Use the rate in effect on the effective date, not on the notice date.

rows.claim: Scenario C — no increase until the 1 Feb 2027 anniversary: 1.4% banked plus 1.6% current.
rows.note: Assumes the 1.4% allowance for the 2/1/2026 anniversary was not used. If it was used, only the 1.6% is available.

rows.claim: The April 2026 addition of a tenant did not create an increase opportunity and did not reset anything.
rows.detail: Rent stayed at $3,995 when P4 joined on 1 Apr 2026. Adding an occupant is not a lawful basis for an increase, and a co-tenant is not subject to a Costa-Hawkins market-rate increase.
rows.note: Also relevant to just cause under Civ. Code 1946.2(a), where a later-added adult tenant changes the 12/24-month test.

rows.claim: The 6.14 / Costa-Hawkins market-rate route is not available while an original tenant remains.
rows.detail: Rule 6.14 requires that the last original occupant has vacated. P1 is still in occupancy.
rows.note: Also, a 6.14 notice must have been served on each subsequent occupant within about 60 days of the landlord knowing of the occupancy — that was not confirmed here. FLAGGED.

rows.claim: Anniversary date and the years available for banking.
rows.detail: Lease start 1 Jun 2019 at $3,150. First increase could have been imposed 1 Jun 2020. No increase has been imposed since. Allowed rates by effective date: 6/1/2020 1.8%; 6/1/2021 0.7%; 6/1/2022 2.3%; 6/1/2023 3.6%; 6/1/2024 1.7%; 6/1/2025 1.4%; 6/1/2026 1.6%.
rows.note: Banking has been permitted since 1 April 1982 (Ord. 37.3(a)(2)), so the whole 2019 tenancy is inside the window.

rows.claim: Total percentage: 13.1%, added and not compounded.
rows.note: The Rent Board's own multiple-year example adds the intervening rates in the same way. Compounding would produce a materially higher and unlawful number.

rows.claim: Dollar increase: $412.65, giving a new base rent of $3,562.65.
rows.note: Cross-check: summing each year's dollar amount on $3,150 gives the same $412.65, which confirms no compounding.

rows.claim: 13.1% exceeds 10%, so 90 days' written notice is required (95 if mailed).
rows.detail: Civ. Code 827(b)(3)(A) and the Rent Board's 90-day rule both trigger above 10%.
rows.note: This is the single most likely procedural error in the Unit 2 file.

rows.claim: The 13.1% figure is the maximum before any petition; a tenant may still dispute the underlying rent history.
rows.detail: The calculation assumes $3,150 on 1 Jun 2019 was the lawful base rent. The petition process requires the full rent history from 1 April 1982, and a tenant may file at any time at no cost.
rows.note: UNVERIFIED in this review: the 2019 lease, any intervening notices, and the licence records were not provided. FLAGGED.

rows.claim: The banking-threshold conflict does not change this result.
rows.detail: The Rent Board's summary page says a skipped increase banks only after 24 months; Rule 4.12 says 12. Every year used for Unit 2 is more than 24 months old, so both readings give 13.1%.
rows.note: FLAGGED at L13 for future years.

rows.claim: A comparable, official 'market rent' benchmark for a 94122 unit was not established.
rows.detail: The Rent Board does not publish rent levels by unit type; HUD FMRs are 40th-percentile gross rents used for voucher payment standards and the FY2026 figure did not render on the HUD page; and the AG and Rent Board tables give percentages, not rents.
rows.note: FLAGGED. No market-rent comparison is asserted anywhere on this site. If a comparable-rent figure is needed, it must come from the Rent Board's comparable-rent petition process (Form 323), not from listing sites.

rows.claim: Neither increase may be served until the rent increase licence exists for that unit.
rows.detail: Housing Inventory reporting generates the licence; for a building of 1-9 units the regime began 1 March 2023. Reporting is annual, due 1 March.
rows.note: UNVERIFIED in this review: licence status for either unit was not provided. FLAGGED.
